newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bereaved Bhutto now faces tests on all fronts.
newsitem.headline: Bereaved Bhutto now faces tests on all fronts.

text.p: Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, grieving for her slain brother, faced the task on Tuesday of halting sectarian unrest after a bloody attack on a Sunni Moslem mosque and the killings of two Shi'ite Moslem leaders.
Bhutto, beset by political, economic and personal troubles, was expected to return to Islamabad after three days of mourning in Karachi and the Bhuttos' home district of Larkana.
Apart from her brother's death and religious tension, she must also cope with a newly assertive President Farooq Leghari, who on Monday demanded a parliamentary probe into corruption.

Leghari, once seen as a loyal Bhutto ally, made clear that he did not agree with her assertion that existing mechanisms were adequate. "The time for action has come," he said in a letter to both houses of parliament.
Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza died in a clash with police in Karachi on Friday. She called his death a conspiracy against their family, but has not identified the culprits.
"Murtaza's enemies are involved in conspiring against the family," Bhutto, flanked by her wailing mother Nusrat and sister Sanam, told mourners at her Karachi residence on Monday.
Bhutto, at odds with her brother while he was alive, described him as a fighter for democracy and said a provincial judicial inquiry would discover the truth about his death.
"Our paths were different but our blood was the same. Our destiny was one - Islam, Pakistan, democracy and equality."
The government must try to prevent further outbreaks of violence after attackers killed 21 worshippers at a Sunni mosque in the Punjab provincial city of Multan on Monday.
Troops in armoured vehicles patrolled Multan after angry crowds stoned Shi'ite neighbourhoods and attacked police.
Gunmen killed a hardline Shi'ite leader in the town of Bahawalpur, 95 km (60 miles) south of Multan, on Sunday night and shot dead another just hours after the mosque attack.
Sunni and Shi'ite militants have waged a bloody vendetta in Pakistan for several years. Shi'ites make up about 15 percent of the country's 130 million people, most of whom are Sunnis.
Tension is running high over the death of Murtaza Bhutto, 42, who had led a splinter faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP), known as PPP-Shaheed Bhutto.
The PPP-Shaheed Bhutto group, accusing the police of deliberately ambushing Murtaza and his companions, has called for nationwide protests against the government for Thursday.
Police fired bullets and teargas to disperse pro-Murtaza demonstrators in the Bhuttos' home town of Larkana in the southern province of Sindh on Monday, wounding two.
